query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying friction stir processing (FSP) to the as‐cast eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve both room-temperature tensile strength and ductility by inducing dynamic recrystallization that disrupts the continuous, brittle lamellar colony interfaces.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that have continuous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Friction Stir Processing (FSP) with a carefully controlled thermal input and tool settings (rotation and traverse speed) to induce dynamic recrystallization at the lamellar interfaces.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing after FSP treatment; processing parameters selected to optimize dynamic recrystallization while avoiding excessive grain growth; the intervention is applied to as-cast eutectic HEA samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined grain structure and disrupted, discontinuous lamellar boundaries due to dynamic recrystallization.
generation.mechanism: FSP generates localized heat and severe plastic deformation, causing dynamic recrystallization that breaks up the continuous lamellar interfaces. This disruption reduces stress concentrations and microcrack nucleation sites, leading to simultaneous enhancements in strength (via grain refinement and increased work hardening) and ductility (through less brittle interfacial behavior).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the FSP-treated alloy will exhibit higher tensile strength and increased room-temperature ductility, reflected in improved yield and ultimate tensile strengths along with greater elongation before fracture.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic HEA with continuous dual-phase lamellar colonies prone to microcrack initiation, which, while strong, suffer from limited ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects depend on optimizing FSP parameters to achieve sufficient dynamic recrystallization without causing grain coarsening; if thermal input is excessive, detrimental coarsening or other microstructural defects may negate the improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of strength and ductility improvements is uncertain and may vary with precise processing conditions and alloy composition; additional optimization and scale-up studies are required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of eutectic HEA samples: one group in the as-cast condition (baseline) and another subjected to FSP under optimized processing conditions. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests on both groups, and perform detailed microstructural analyses (e.g., SEM/TEM) to assess grain structure, boundary characteristics, and crack formation sites.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FSP-treated samples do not demonstrate statistically significant simultaneous increases in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the as-cast baseline, or if microstructural analysis does not reveal a disrupted lamellar architecture (i.e., dynamic recrystallization fails to occur as intended), the hypothesis is falsified.

While such microstructures and their effects associated with conventional thermomechanical processing on the deformation behavior in HEAs, including TRIP HEAs, have been investigated in detail, studies on severe plastic deformation, such as equal channel angular pressing (ECAP), high-pressure torsion (HPT) and friction stir processing (FSP), of HEAs and their effects on the mechanical properties have been limited so far. Among these techniques, FSP is the most industrially feasible process for bulk products and has applicability for solid state joining. Earlier work by Kumar et al. showed that FSP of Al0.1CoCrFeNi HEA resulted in substantial improvement of strength and ductility when compared with the as-cast condition, due to enhanced grain refinement and a greater fraction of high angle grain boundaries. frame.system: Eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries formed via conventional processing, which creates a baseline microstructure prone to microcracking.
frame.goal: Achieve a single processing intervention that simultaneously improves tensile strength and room-temperature ductility by mitigating microcrack initiation at internal boundaries.
frame.limitation: Conventional processing increases strength at the expense of ductility and has not eliminated the intrinsic brittleness due to microcrack nucleation along the numerous lamellar colony interfaces.

conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility
constraints: single intervention must improve both strength and ductility
outcomes must be defined relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline
boundary conditions (processing parameters) must be identified
intervention should be testable and falsifiable via a targeted experiment
prior_attempts: Various microstructural-design strategies and processing methods aimed at modifying the lamellar architecture have been proposed, yet none have eliminated the trade-off between high strength and low room-temperature ductility.
frame.hypothesis: I hypothesize that applying friction stir processing (FSP) to the as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy will refine its dual-phase lamellar microstructure by inducing dynamic recrystallization at the internal boundaries. This will reduce the continuity and stress concentration at these interfaces, thereby suppressing microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile loading. Relative to the unmodified baseline, the FSP-treated alloy is expected to display both enhanced strength—due to refined grain structures and increased work hardening—and improved ductility because of the reduced brittleness at the colony boundaries. The boundary condition for success is that the processing parameters must achieve sufficient thermal input to induce recrystallization without causing overgrowth or coarsening of grains. Supporting evidence comes from analogous studies in other alloy systems where FSP has improved mechanical properties through microstructural refinement. An experiment to test (and potentially falsify) this hypothesis would involve treating samples with precisely controlled FSP parameters, followed by systematic room-temperature tensile tests combined with microstructural analysis (e.g., electron microscopy) to compare crack density, grain size, and mechanical performance against untreated controls. If the FSP-treated samples do not show simultaneous improvements in tensile strength and ductility or if detrimental grain coarsening occurs, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC4145285) established eutectic high‐entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar microstructures that already demonstrated interesting strength–ductility combinations but suffered from inherent microcracking at numerous colony boundaries. Subsequent studies (PMC5818523) applied cryo‐rolling and annealing to refine the lamellar architecture, achieving partial success by refining grain sizes; however, the intrinsic connectivity of the lamellae still permitted stress concentrations that initiate cracks. Parallel efforts using tailored thermo‐mechanical treatments (PMC6353877 and PMC6687781) introduced dual or hierarchical microstructural heterogeneities to further enhance mechanical performance. Notably, friction stir processing (FSP) was explored (PMC5701024) as a route to dynamically recrystallize regions at internal interfaces, disrupting continuous boundaries, refining grain structure, and thus simultaneously enhancing strength and ductility. Overall, while processing interventions and microstructural design modifications have progressively targeted grain refinement and heterogeneous phase distribution, the persistent issue of microcrack nucleation at continuous lamellar colony interfaces remains a central limitation.
decision.unsolved: Despite the advances from thermo-mechanical treatments and even friction stir processing in dual-phase HEAs, the specific problem of continuous internal boundaries acting as stress concentrators and microcrack nucleation sites in the as-cast lamellar colonies remains unsolved. In other words, previous approaches have not definitively broken up or sufficiently disrupted the interconnectivity of the lamellae to mitigate microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation while preserving or enhancing tensile strength.
decision.lever: Friction Stir Processing (FSP) with controlled thermal input to induce dynamic recrystallization along lamellar colony boundaries
decision.why: Building on the trend observed in prior work – where traditional thermo-mechanical treatments and even initial FSP studies have refined microstructures but did not fully eliminate continuous, brittle interfaces – the application of a precisely controlled FSP intervention is the most plausible next step. The hypothesis is that by tuning FSP processing parameters (e.g., tool rotation, traverse speed, and heat input) to optimize dynamic recrystallization, one can disrupt the continuity of the lamellar colonies. This disruption should relieve stress concentrations at internal boundaries and hence suppress microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile loading, achieving simultaneous enhancements in strength and ductility relative to the unmodified baseline.
